claim: Levels of alertness are closely linked with human behavior and cognition.
source: Levels of alertness are closely linked with human behavior and cognition.
evidence: This is a general statement presented in the abstract that establishes the motivation for the study.

claim: An fMRI alertness marker calculated in a short pre-stimulus interval captures trial-to-trial behavioral responses to incoming sensory stimuli.
source: We demonstrate that this fMRI alertness marker, calculated in a short pre-stimulus interval, captures trial-to-trial behavioral responses to incoming sensory stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results shown in Figures 3 and 4, where pre-stimulus fMRI alertness index differs between hits/misses and fast/slow responses.

claim: The prediction of both EEG and behavioral responses during the task may be accomplished using only a small fraction of fMRI voxels.
source: In addition, we find that the prediction of both EEG and behavioral responses during the task may be accomplished using only a small fraction of fMRI voxels.
evidence: This is supported by the template thresholding experiment shown in Figure 5, demonstrating that using only 1% of voxels maintains predictive power.

claim: Accounting for alertness appears to increase the statistical detection of task-activated brain areas.
source: Furthermore, we observe that accounting for alertness appears to increase the statistical detection of task-activated brain areas.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 6, where including the fMRI alertness index as a covariate increases t-scores in task-relevant regions.

claim: Behavioral responses can change even across repeated presentations of the same stimulus.
source: Behavioral responses can change even across repeated presentations of the same stimulus, and altered levels of neural variability may index individual differences in cognitive function (Dinstein et al., 2015; van Kempen et al., 2019; Cohen, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Altered levels of neural variability may index individual differences in cognitive function.
source: Behavioral responses can change even across repeated presentations of the same stimulus, and altered levels of neural variability may index individual differences in cognitive function (Dinstein et al., 2015; van Kempen et al., 2019; Cohen, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to three studies examining neural variability and cognitive function.

claim: One major determinant of behavioral and neural variability is the brain's continuously fluctuating level of arousal.
source: One major determinant of behavioral and neural variability is the brain's continuously fluctuating level of arousal, referring to the dimension of functional states linked with phenomena including alert wakefulness, drowsiness, and sleep.
evidence: This is a general statement establishing the theoretical framework, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: Levels of arousal closely interact with processes underlying decision-making.
source: Growing evidence indicates that levels of arousal closely interact with processes underlying decision-making (van Kempen et al., 2019), visuomotor performance (Makeig et al., 2000; Poudel et al., 2018), perception (Mather and Sutherland, 2011), and attention (Foucher et al., 2004), motivating incorporation of arousal levels into models of healthy and pathological brain function (Lee et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2012; Englot et al., 2008; Motelow et al., 2015; Salomon et al., 2011; Nashiro and Mather, 2011; Jawinski et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van Kempen et al., 2019.

claim: Levels of arousal closely interact with visuomotor performance.
source: Growing evidence indicates that levels of arousal closely interact with processes underlying decision-making (van Kempen et al., 2019), visuomotor performance (Makeig et al., 2000; Poudel et al., 2018), perception (Mather and Sutherland, 2011), and attention (Foucher et al., 2004), motivating incorporation of arousal levels into models of healthy and pathological brain function (Lee et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2012; Englot et al., 2008; Motelow et al., 2015; Salomon et al., 2011; Nashiro and Mather, 2011; Jawinski et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Makeig et al., 2000 and Poudel et al., 2018.

claim: Levels of arousal closely interact with perception.
source: Growing evidence indicates that levels of arousal closely interact with processes underlying decision-making (van Kempen et al., 2019), visuomotor performance (Makeig et al., 2000; Poudel et al., 2018), perception (Mather and Sutherland, 2011), and attention (Foucher et al., 2004), motivating incorporation of arousal levels into models of healthy and pathological brain function (Lee et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2012; Englot et al., 2008; Motelow et al., 2015; Salomon et al., 2011; Nashiro and Mather, 2011; Jawinski et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mather and Sutherland, 2011.

claim: Levels of arousal closely interact with attention.
source: Growing evidence indicates that levels of arousal closely interact with processes underlying decision-making (van Kempen et al., 2019), visuomotor performance (Makeig et al., 2000; Poudel et al., 2018), perception (Mather and Sutherland, 2011), and attention (Foucher et al., 2004), motivating incorporation of arousal levels into models of healthy and pathological brain function (Lee et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2012; Englot et al., 2008; Motelow et al., 2015; Salomon et al., 2011; Nashiro and Mather, 2011; Jawinski et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Foucher et al., 2004.

claim: Variations in attentional responses have been linked to fluctuations in spontaneous fMRI signals.
source: For example, variations in attentional (Rosenberg et al., 2016), motor, (Fox et al., 2006), and perceptual (Sadaghiani et al., 2009) responses, have been linked to fluctuations in spontaneous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) signals, observed both in focal regions of the brain (Fox et al., 2006; Sadaghiani et al., 2009; Hesselmann et al., 2008a; Hesselmann et al., 2008b) and in large-scale network structure (Rosenberg et al., 2016; Sadaghiani et al., 2009; Kelly et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2013; Sadaghiani et al., 2015; Boly et al., 2007; Coste et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rosenberg et al., 2016.

claim: Variations in motor responses have been linked to fluctuations in spontaneous fMRI signals.
source: For example, variations in attentional (Rosenberg et al., 2016), motor, (Fox et al., 2006), and perceptual (Sadaghiani et al., 2009) responses, have been linked to fluctuations in spontaneous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) signals, observed both in focal regions of the brain (Fox et al., 2006; Sadaghiani et al., 2009; Hesselmann et al., 2008a; Hesselmann et al., 2008b) and in large-scale network structure (Rosenberg et al., 2016; Sadaghiani et al., 2009; Kelly et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2013; Sadaghiani et al., 2015; Boly et al., 2007; Coste et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fox et al., 2006.

claim: Variations in perceptual responses have been linked to fluctuations in spontaneous fMRI signals.
source: For example, variations in attentional (Rosenberg et al., 2016), motor, (Fox et al., 2006), and perceptual (Sadaghiani et al., 2009) responses, have been linked to fluctuations in spontaneous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) signals, observed both in focal regions of the brain (Fox et al., 2006; Sadaghiani et al., 2009; Hesselmann et al., 2008a; Hesselmann et al., 2008b) and in large-scale network structure (Rosenberg et al., 2016; Sadaghiani et al., 2009; Kelly et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2013; Sadaghiani et al., 2015; Boly et al., 2007; Coste et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sadaghiani et al., 2009.

claim: Temporal variation in spontaneous fMRI signals and connectivity have been found to be altered in neuropsychiatric disorders as well as in aging.
source: Temporal variation in spontaneous fMRI signals and connectivity have also been found to be altered in neuropsychiatric disorders as well as in aging (Yang et al., 2014; Nomi et al., 2017; Calhoun et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2014; Nomi et al., 2017; and Calhoun et al., 2014.

claim: Relatively few fMRI studies have examined the specific role of dynamically fluctuating arousal states in shaping ongoing neural or behavioral variability.
source: However, relatively few fMRI studies have examined the specific role of dynamically fluctuating arousal states in shaping ongoing neural or behavioral variability (Dinstein et al., 2015; Liu and Falahpour, 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Distinct EEG-defined sleep stages may be classified based on fMRI correlation patterns calculated across 1–2 min sliding windows.
source: Prior work on the detection of arousal states from fMRI alone has demonstrated that distinct EEG-defined sleep stages may be classified based on fMRI correlation patterns calculated across 1–2 min sliding windows (Tagliazucchi and Laufs, 2014; Tagliazucchi et al., 2012; Altmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tagliazucchi and Laufs, 2014; Tagliazucchi et al., 2012; and Altmann et al., 2016.

claim: Many subjects can begin to lose wakefulness even within the first few minutes of an fMRI scan.
source: Moreover, it was found that many subjects can begin to lose wakefulness even within the first few minutes of an fMRI scan (Tagliazucchi and Laufs, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tagliazucchi and Laufs, 2014.

claim: Dynamic connectivity patterns calculated in 40 s sliding windows track slow variations in subjects' performance in an auditory vigilance task.
source: Focusing on levels of arousal across the waking state, Wang et al., 2016 identified dynamic connectivity patterns, calculated in 40 s sliding windows, whose expression at each window tracked slow variations in subjects' performance in an auditory vigilance task.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: The fMRI arousal index was found to correlate with intracranial electrophysiological arousal and spontaneous eye opening/closing in macaque monkeys.
source: The extracted 'fMRI arousal index' was found to correlate with intracranial electrophysiological arousal and spontaneous eye opening/closing in macaque monkeys (Chang et al., 2016), as well as with scalp EEG in human subjects (Falahpour et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2016.

claim: The fMRI arousal index was found to correlate with scalp EEG in human subjects.
source: The extracted 'fMRI arousal index' was found to correlate with intracranial electrophysiological arousal and spontaneous eye opening/closing in macaque monkeys (Chang et al., 2016), as well as with scalp EEG in human subjects (Falahpour et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Falahpour et al., 2018.

claim: The fMRI alertness index tracks continuous variations in EEG alertness.
source: fMRI-derived alertness index tracks continuous variations in EEG alertness
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2, showing temporal cross-correlation between fMRI and EEG alertness indices.

claim: The fMRI alertness index (red) is compared with an established EEG vigilance index (the alpha/theta power ratio, convolved with a hemodynamic response function; blue).
source: (B) To assess the ability to predict electrophysiological alertness in the task scan, the estimated fMRI alertness index (red) is compared with an established EEG vigilance index that was collected simultaneously (the alpha/theta power ratio, convolved with a hemodynamic response function; blue).
evidence: This describes the methodology shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The temporal cross-correlation between the fMRI alertness index and EEG alertness index is significantly different from a null distribution created by randomly permuting the indices across task scans.
source: Figure 2C shows the temporal cross-correlation between these two waveforms across the set of task scans, relative to a null distribution that was created by randomly permuting the fMRI alertness index and EEG alertness index across the task scans.
evidence: Figure 2C shows the cross-correlation is elevated above the null distribution, indicating statistical significance.

claim: Hit trials are associated with greater power in the alpha band (8–12 Hz) in the EEG spectrogram, consistent with increased arousal.
source: The event-locked EEG spectrogram showed clear evidence that hit and miss trials were accompanied by distinct arousal states, with the hit spectrogram showing greater power in the alpha band (8–12 Hz, consistent with increased arousal, particularly at stimulus onset) and the miss spectrogram showing greater power in the lower frequency bands commonly associated with increased drowsiness or sleep (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the EEG spectrogram data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Miss trials are associated with greater power in lower frequency bands commonly associated with increased drowsiness or sleep.
source: The event-locked EEG spectrogram showed clear evidence that hit and miss trials were accompanied by distinct arousal states, with the hit spectrogram showing greater power in the alpha band (8–12 Hz, consistent with increased arousal, particularly at stimulus onset) and the miss spectrogram showing greater power in the lower frequency bands commonly associated with increased drowsiness or sleep (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the EEG spectrogram data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The fMRI alertness index predicted significantly greater levels of alertness in hits compared to misses in the pre-stimulus interval (5 s prior to stimulus onset).
source: Across subjects, the fMRI alertness index predicted significantly greater levels of alertness in hits compared to misses, both within the pre-stimulus interval (5 s prior to stimulus onset; light gray region) and post-stimulus interval (10 s after stimulus onset; striped gray region).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (p=3.34e-03, effect size d=1.24) and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The fMRI alertness index predicted significantly greater levels of alertness in hits compared to misses in the post-stimulus interval (10 s after stimulus onset).
source: Across subjects, the fMRI alertness index predicted significantly greater levels of alertness in hits compared to misses, both within the pre-stimulus interval (5 s prior to stimulus onset; light gray region) and post-stimulus interval (10 s after stimulus onset; striped gray region).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis (p=6.40e-06, d=2.39) and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Significant differences between hits and misses were observed in the pre-stimulus interval (p=3.34e-03, effect size [Cohen's d] = 1.24).
source: Significant differences between hits and misses were observed in both the pre-stimulus (p=3.34e-03, effect size [Cohen's d] = 1.24) and post-stimulus (p=6.40e-06, d = 2.39) intervals, defined, respectively, as the intervals 5 s before, and 10 s after, the stimulus onset (Figure 3B; two-sample t-tests).
evidence: This is a statistical result from two-sample t-tests comparing hits and misses.

claim: Significant differences between hits and misses were observed in the post-stimulus interval (p=6.40e-06, d = 2.39).
source: Significant differences between hits and misses were observed in both the pre-stimulus (p=3.34e-03, effect size [Cohen's d] = 1.24) and post-stimulus (p=6.40e-06, d = 2.39) intervals, defined, respectively, as the intervals 5 s before, and 10 s after, the stimulus onset (Figure 3B; two-sample t-tests).
evidence: This is a statistical result from two-sample t-tests comparing hits and misses.

claim: Within individual subjects, trials with hits were associated with higher levels of the fMRI alertness index in the pre-stimulus interval compared to trials with misses (t(8)=3.35, p=0.01, paired t-test; d = 1.11).
source: Within individual subjects, trials with hits were associated with higher levels of the fMRI alertness index in the pre-stimulus interval compared to trials with misses (Figure 3C). Of those subjects who had both hits and misses, all but two followed the expected trend, and the differences between hits and misses were significant (t(8)=3.35, p=0.01, paired t-test; d = 1.11).
evidence: This is supported by paired t-test statistics and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fast hits were associated with higher levels of the pre-stimulus fMRI alertness index compared to slow hits (t(9)=4.52, p=0.001, paired t-test; Cohen's d = 1.43).
source: Within the 10 subjects that had both fast hits and slow hits, fast hits were associated with higher levels of the pre-stimulus fMRI alertness index compared to slow hits (t(9)=4.52, p=0.001, paired t-test; Cohen's d = 1.43; Figure 4A), and all showed higher mean values during fast compared to slow hit trials.
evidence: This is supported by paired t-test statistics and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: All subjects with both fast and slow hits showed higher mean fMRI alertness index values during fast compared to slow hit trials.
source: Within the 10 subjects that had both fast hits and slow hits, fast hits were associated with higher levels of the pre-stimulus fMRI alertness index compared to slow hits (t(9)=4.52, p=0.001, paired t-test; Cohen's d = 1.43; Figure 4A), and all showed higher mean values during fast compared to slow hit trials.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the data analysis.

claim: In the pre-stimulus interval, both the EEG alpha/theta ratio and the fMRI alertness index showed a main effect of behavioral response across subjects (p<0.05, one-way ANOVA).
source: In the pre-stimulus interval, both the EEG alpha/theta ratio and the fMRI alertness index showed a main effect of behavioral response across subjects; p<0.05, (one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by one-way ANOVA statistics and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the pre-stimulus interval, Tukey–Kramer post hoc tests indicated pairwise differences for fast hits versus slow hits for EEG (p<0.05).
source: Tukey–Kramer post hoc tests, controlled for multiple comparisons, indicated pairwise differences for fast hits (orange) versus slow hits (yellow) for EEG and between fast hits and misses (blue) for both EEG and fMRI (*p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by post hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the pre-stimulus interval, Tukey–Kramer post hoc tests indicated pairwise differences between fast hits and misses for both EEG and fMRI (p<0.05).
source: Tukey–Kramer post hoc tests, controlled for multiple comparisons, indicated pairwise differences for fast hits (orange) versus slow hits (yellow) for EEG and between fast hits and misses (blue) for both EEG and fMRI (*p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by post hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the post-stimulus interval, a main effect of behavioral response was found for both EEG and fMRI.
source: In the 10 s post-stimulus interval, there was also a main effect of behavioral response for both EEG alpha/theta and the fMRI alertness index (EEG: F(2) = 8.82, p=0.1e-02, fMRI: F(2) = 14.12, p=5.75e-05; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by one-way ANOVA statistics (EEG: F(2) = 8.82, p=0.1e-02, fMRI: F(2) = 14.12, p=5.75e-05) and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In the post-stimulus interval, both EEG and fMRI showed post hoc pairwise differences between both fast and slow responses compared to misses (p<0.05).
source: Both EEG and fMRI showed post hoc pairwise differences between both fast and slow responses compared to misses, and neither showed a difference between fast and slow hits.
evidence: This is supported by post hoc statistical tests shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Neither EEG nor fMRI showed a difference between fast and slow hits in the post-stimulus interval.
source: Both EEG and fMRI showed post hoc pairwise differences between both fast and slow responses compared to misses, and neither showed a difference between fast and slow hits.
evidence: This is a negative finding from post hoc statistical tests.

claim: The whole-brain vigilance template could be reduced to its top ~1% of positive and negative voxels without considerable loss in predictive power in macaque monkeys.
source: In a previous study of macaque monkeys, we demonstrated that the whole-brain vigilance template could be reduced to its top ~1% of positive and negative voxels without considerable loss in predictive power (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2016.

claim: Retaining voxels of both positive and negative signs was found to be critical for vigilance prediction in macaque monkeys.
source: In addition, despite the much larger number of negative compared to positive voxels, retaining voxels of both signs was found to be critical (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2016.

claim: When jointly including positive and negative voxels, there was little change in the predictive power of the fMRI alertness index, even at thresholds down to 1%.
source: By contrast, when jointly including positive and negative voxels, we found that there was little change in the predictive power, even at thresholds down to 1%.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A, showing that the joint positive and negative template maintains performance at 1% of voxels.

claim: The highest-magnitude (top 1%) voxels with negative sign were localized mainly to primary visual, auditory, and sensory/motor cortices.
source: Here, the highest-magnitude (top 1%) voxels with negative sign were localized mainly to primary visual, auditory, and sensory/motor cortices, and those with the highest-magnitude positive sign were found in the ventricles (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The highest-magnitude (top 1%) voxels with positive sign were found in the ventricles.
source: Here, the highest-magnitude (top 1%) voxels with negative sign were localized mainly to primary visual, auditory, and sensory/motor cortices, and those with the highest-magnitude positive sign were found in the ventricles (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the spatial analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The fMRI alertness index generated from the reduced template (top 1% positive, top 1% negative voxels) showed a significant main effect of behavioral response in the pre-stimulus interval (F(2)=10.09, p=0.0005).
source: The fMRI alertness index generated from the reduced template (top 1% positive, top 1% negative voxels), calculated in the pre-stimulus interval, showed a significant main effect of behavioral response (F(2)=10.09, p=0.0005; Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by one-way ANOVA statistics and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A small fraction of voxels may suffice for detecting fluctuations in alertness.
source: This finding suggests that despite the broad nature of arousal-related signal changes across the brain, the information is inherently low dimensional, and a small fraction of voxels may suffice for detecting fluctuations in alertness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the template thresholding experiment results shown in Figure 5.

claim: A model that included only the event-related task responses resulted in weak activation in the expected bilateral auditory and left motor regions.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, a model that included only the event-related task responses resulted in weak activation in the expected bilateral auditory and left motor regions, along with negative BOLD signal change in a number of cortical regions, with some resemblance to the pattern of correlations with EEG arousal (Figure 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A model that included only the event-related task responses resulted in negative BOLD signal change in a number of cortical regions.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, a model that included only the event-related task responses resulted in weak activation in the expected bilateral auditory and left motor regions, along with negative BOLD signal change in a number of cortical regions, with some resemblance to the pattern of correlations with EEG arousal (Figure 1, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Including the fMRI alertness index as a covariate reduced the negative responses and increased t-scores in bilateral auditory cortex, left motor cortex, and the contralateral cerebellum.
source: Including the fMRI alertness index as a covariate reduced the negative responses and increased t-scores in bilateral auditory cortex, left motor cortex (the region expected to be associated with right-handed button presses), and the contralateral cerebellum (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Including the fMRI alertness index as a covariate markedly increased the activation in areas associated with the 'salience network' (including the anterior cingulate cortex and insula).
source: Interestingly, this covariate also markedly increased the activation in areas associated with the 'salience network' (including the anterior cingulate cortex and insula [Menon and Uddin, 2010], which are known to co-activate with externally salient or oddball stimuli Crottaz-Herbette and Menon, 2006); this may perhaps to be expected given the long and unpredictable inter-stimulus intervals in this task.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 6B, with interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The anterior cingulate cortex and insula are known to co-activate with externally salient or oddball stimuli.
source: Interestingly, this covariate also markedly increased the activation in areas associated with the 'salience network' (including the anterior cingulate cortex and insula [Menon and Uddin, 2010], which are known to co-activate with externally salient or oddball stimuli Crottaz-Herbette and Menon, 2006); this may perhaps to be expected given the long and unpredictable inter-stimulus intervals in this task.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Crottaz-Herbette and Menon, 2006.

claim: Using the EEG alertness index as a regressor reduced the negative activation and increased the t-statistics in auditory, motor, and salience areas.
source: Using the EEG alertness index as a regressor also reduced the negative activation and increased the t-statistics in auditory, motor, and salience areas (Figure 6C), though surprisingly, to a somewhat lesser extent than with the fMRI index.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the GLM analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The lasso model yielded correlations with the EEG alertness index that were similar to, though slightly lower than, those generated by the template-based approach.
source: The lasso model yielded correlations with the EEG alertness index that were similar to, though slightly lower than, those generated by the template-based approach (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the lasso regression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The lasso model that was trained on fMRI time series from a 268-region atlas was superior to that which used the time series from all voxels as input.
source: Furthermore, the lasso model that was trained on fMRI time series from a 268-region atlas (Shen et al., 2013) was superior to that which used the time series from all voxels as input.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the lasso regression analysis.

claim: Time-resolved predictions of alertness, directly estimated in fMRI data without the need for simultaneous EEG, may capture inter-trial behavioral responses and continuous internal state variations.
source: In conclusion, our results indicate that time-resolved predictions of alertness, directly estimated in fMRI data without the need for simultaneous EEG, may capture inter-trial behavioral responses and continuous internal state variations.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Changes in arousal are coordinated by ascending projections from the brainstem, via regions including thalamus, basal forebrain regions, and posterior hypothalamus.
source: Changes in arousal are coordinated by ascending projections from the brainstem, via regions including thalamus, basal forebrain regions, and posterior hypothalamus (Jones, 2005; Saper et al., 2005), and manifest in altered responsiveness to sensory stimuli (Ogilvie, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jones, 2005 and Saper et al., 2005.

claim: Changes in arousal manifest in altered responsiveness to sensory stimuli.
source: Changes in arousal are coordinated by ascending projections from the brainstem, via regions including thalamus, basal forebrain regions, and posterior hypothalamus (Jones, 2005; Saper et al., 2005), and manifest in altered responsiveness to sensory stimuli (Ogilvie, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ogilvie, 2001.

claim: During periods of drowsiness and light sleep, large-amplitude and extensive fMRI signal changes have been observed in which much of the cortex is modulated together, and certain subcortical structures (including the thalamus) display opposing fluctuations.
source: During periods of drowsiness and light sleep, large-amplitude and extensive fMRI signal changes have been observed in which much of the cortex is modulated together, and certain subcortical structures (including the thalamus) display opposing fluctuations (Chang et al., 2016; Falahpour et al., 2018; Olbrich et al., 2009; Goldman et al., 2002; Moosmann et al., 2003; Ong et al., 2015; Poudel et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2012; Feige et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Higher levels of pre-stimulus activity in the default-mode network and/or salience (cingulo-opercular) network, and lower levels in task-positive/dorsal attention networks, have been associated with auditory stimulus detection.
source: In particular, higher levels of pre-stimulus activity in the default-mode network and/or salience (cingulo-opercular) network, and lower levels in task-positive/dorsal attention networks, have been associated with auditory stimulus detection (Sadaghiani et al., 2009) and faster reaction times in visual psychomotor vigilance task (Thompson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sadaghiani et al., 2009.

claim: Higher levels of pre-stimulus activity in the default-mode network and/or salience (cingulo-opercular) network, and lower levels in task-positive/dorsal attention networks, have been associated with faster reaction times in visual psychomotor vigilance task.
source: In particular, higher levels of pre-stimulus activity in the default-mode network and/or salience (cingulo-opercular) network, and lower levels in task-positive/dorsal attention networks, have been associated with auditory stimulus detection (Sadaghiani et al., 2009) and faster reaction times in visual psychomotor vigilance task (Thompson et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thompson et al., 2013.

claim: Retaining even just 1% of positive voxels and 1% of the negative voxels produced only a 5.7% decrease in performance on average (in terms of correlation with EEG alertness).
source: Indeed, we found that retaining even just 1% of positive voxels and 1% of the negative voxels produced only a 5.7% decrease in performance on average (in terms of correlation with EEG alertness).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the template thresholding experiment.

claim: A joint pattern of positive and negative voxels may be most critical for decoding arousal with the present approach.
source: This effect suggests that a joint pattern of positive and negative voxels may be most critical for decoding arousal with the present approach, consistent with our prior results in macaque monkeys (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference from the data, supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The strongest positive voxels in the template (those which had the greatest positive correlation with alertness) were localized to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
source: However, unlike in the macaque study, where the strongest positive voxels in the template (i.e., those which had the greatest positive correlation with alertness) were localized to thalamus, here we found the strongest positive correlations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), though weaker positive clusters were also found in mediodorsal thalamus and anterior cingulate cortex.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the spatial analysis of the template.

claim: Weaker positive clusters were also found in mediodorsal thalamus and anterior cingulate cortex.
source: However, unlike in the macaque study, where the strongest positive voxels in the template (i.e., those which had the greatest positive correlation with alertness) were localized to thalamus, here we found the strongest positive correlations in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), though weaker positive clusters were also found in mediodorsal thalamus and anterior cingulate cortex.
evidence: This is a descriptive finding from the spatial analysis of the template.

claim: Positive correlations between an arousal index and CSF have been seen in prior human EEG–fMRI studies that use a continuous EEG power ratio (alpha to theta and delta bands).
source: Positive correlations between an arousal index and CSF have been seen in prior human EEG–fMRI studies that use a continuous EEG power ratio (alpha to theta and delta bands Falahpour et al., 2018) and discrete EEG-defined vigilance staging (Olbrich et al., 2009), where ventricular signals in the latter were suggested to potentially relate to effects of heart rate (HR) on fMRI data (de Munck et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Falahpour et al., 2018 and Olbrich et al., 2009.

claim: Ventricular signals were suggested to potentially relate to effects of heart rate (HR) on fMRI data.
source: Positive correlations between an arousal index and CSF have been seen in prior human EEG–fMRI studies that use a continuous EEG power ratio (alpha to theta and delta bands Falahpour et al., 2018) and discrete EEG-defined vigilance staging (Olbrich et al., 2009), where ventricular signals in the latter were suggested to potentially relate to effects of heart rate (HR) on fMRI data (de Munck et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to de Munck et al., 2008.

claim: A pattern with opposing gray-matter and ventricular signals was reported to comprise the first principal component of the global fMRI signal that is modulated by sleep depth.
source: A pattern very similar to the reduced template, with opposing gray-matter and ventricular signals, was also reported to comprise the first principal component of the global fMRI signal that is modulated by sleep depth (McAvoy et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to McAvoy et al., 2019.

claim: An inverse relationship between CSF and gray-matter signals has been found to correlate with EEG during sleep.
source: An inverse relationship between CSF and gray-matter signals has also been found to correlate with EEG (Fultz et al., 2019), and both EEG and autonomic responses (Özbay et al., 2019), during sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fultz et al., 2019.

claim: An inverse relationship between CSF and gray-matter signals has been found to correlate with both EEG and autonomic responses during sleep.
source: An inverse relationship between CSF and gray-matter signals has also been found to correlate with EEG (Fultz et al., 2019), and both EEG and autonomic responses (Özbay et al., 2019), during sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Özbay et al., 2019.

claim: Widespread fMRI signal changes, generated by either neuronal or autonomic activity, lead to antagonistic fMRI signal changes in the downstream venous vasculature, in part due to a disjoint timing and amplitude relationship of blood volume and blood oxygenation effects.
source: One mechanistic explanation offered recently is that widespread fMRI signal changes, generated by either neuronal or autonomic activity, lead to antagonistic fMRI signal changes in the downstream venous vasculature, in part due to a disjoint timing and amplitude relationship of blood volume and blood oxygenation effects (Özbay et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Özbay et al., 2018.

claim: Fluctuations in arousal are closely coupled with physiological changes, such as changes in HR and respiratory patterns.
source: Fluctuations in arousal are closely coupled with physiological changes, such as changes in HR and respiratory patterns (Özbay et al., 2019; Yuan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Özbay et al., 2019 and Yuan et al., 2013.

claim: Projecting out low-frequency fluctuations in HR and RV generally reduced the correlation between the fMRI and EEG alertness measures.
source: In additional experiments, we found that projecting out low-frequency fluctuations in HR and RV generally reduced the correlation between the fMRI and EEG alertness measures (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Materials and methods), suggesting that retaining low-frequency systemic physiological components may present useful information when the goal is to extract arousal fluctuations from the fMRI data.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Retaining low-frequency systemic physiological components may present useful information when the goal is to extract arousal fluctuations from the fMRI data.
source: In additional experiments, we found that projecting out low-frequency fluctuations in HR and RV generally reduced the correlation between the fMRI and EEG alertness measures (Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and Materials and methods), suggesting that retaining low-frequency systemic physiological components may present useful information when the goal is to extract arousal fluctuations from the fMRI data.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the physiological regression experiment.

claim: The whole-brain template overlaps very closely with a spatial pattern linked with sympathetic arousal in stage-2 sleep.
source: The whole-brain template derived here also overlaps very closely with a spatial pattern linked with sympathetic arousal in stage-2 sleep (Özbay et al., 2019; Özbay et al., 2018) as well as in drowsy wakefulness and stage-1 sleep (Chang et al., 2018), whereby gray-matter regions (predominantly primary sensory cortex) are anti-correlated with BOLD signal in deep white matter and CSF.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Özbay et al., 2019 and Özbay et al., 2018.

claim: The whole-brain template overlaps very closely with a spatial pattern linked with sympathetic arousal in drowsy wakefulness and stage-1 sleep.
source: The whole-brain template derived here also overlaps very closely with a spatial pattern linked with sympathetic arousal in stage-2 sleep (Özbay et al., 2019; Özbay et al., 2018) as well as in drowsy wakefulness and stage-1 sleep (Chang et al., 2018), whereby gray-matter regions (predominantly primary sensory cortex) are anti-correlated with BOLD signal in deep white matter and CSF.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2018.

claim: The template map may reflect in part the concurrent modulation of central and peripheral arousal, and their systemic physiological correlates.
source: Our template map may, therefore, reflect in part the concurrent modulation of central and peripheral arousal, and their systemic physiological correlates.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the template map's physiological basis.

claim: Natural drifts in wakefulness are common during fMRI.
source: While it is widely recognized that natural drifts in wakefulness are common during fMRI, few studies explicitly model dynamic arousal fluctuations in standard fMRI task analyses, as concurrent EEG and pupillometry is relatively uncommon during routine fMRI scans.
evidence: This is a statement about common knowledge in the field.

claim: Few studies explicitly model dynamic arousal fluctuations in standard fMRI task analyses.
source: While it is widely recognized that natural drifts in wakefulness are common during fMRI, few studies explicitly model dynamic arousal fluctuations in standard fMRI task analyses, as concurrent EEG and pupillometry is relatively uncommon during routine fMRI scans.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Concurrent EEG and pupillometry is relatively uncommon during routine fMRI scans.
source: While it is widely recognized that natural drifts in wakefulness are common during fMRI, few studies explicitly model dynamic arousal fluctuations in standard fMRI task analyses, as concurrent EEG and pupillometry is relatively uncommon during routine fMRI scans.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in fMRI studies.

claim: The approach currently detects primarily relative, rather than absolute, levels of alertness across a scan.
source: One is that it currently detects primarily relative, rather than absolute, levels of alertness across a scan.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the method.

claim: The fMRI alertness index is restricted between −1 and 1 because spatial correlation is used to determine a frame-by-frame alertness measure.
source: Since spatial correlation is used to determine a frame-by-frame alertness measure, the fMRI alertness index is restricted between −1 and 1.
evidence: This is a methodological constraint of the approach.

claim: The fMRI alertness index may not detect slower baseline shifts in alertness because fMRI signals are often detrended to remove scanner artifacts.
source: In addition, as fMRI signals are often detrended to remove scanner artifacts, such an index may not detect slower baseline shifts in alertness.
evidence: This is a stated limitation based on preprocessing steps.

claim: Inter-subject and inter-scan differences in the performance of fMRI alertness estimation have been observed.
source: In addition, we and others observe inter-subject and inter-scan differences in the performance of fMRI alertness estimation (Falahpour et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Falahpour et al., 2018 and the authors' own observations.

claim: Such differences may partially reflect the degree of alertness fluctuation present in the fMRI data itself (with greater modulation of alertness lending itself to better prediction).
source: Such differences may partially reflect the degree of alertness fluctuation present in the fMRI data itself (with greater modulation of alertness lending itself to better prediction), but these questions are currently under investigation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed variability.

claim: The small sample size is a key limitation of this study.
source: One key limitation of this study is the small sample size.
evidence: This is an explicitly stated limitation.

claim: The effect sizes of the current results may be overestimated due to the small sample size.
source: As a result, the effect sizes of the current results may be overestimated, and findings may not generalize well to the population from which they are sampled.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the small sample size.

claim: Findings may not generalize well to the population from which they are sampled due to the small sample size.
source: As a result, the effect sizes of the current results may be overestimated, and findings may not generalize well to the population from which they are sampled.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of the small sample size.

claim: The scans are long (24.5 min per scan).
source: Nonetheless, there are several factors that increase our confidence in the present results: our scans are long (24.5 min per scan), and the replication analyses carried out in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 4 further support the generalizability of this approach.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Simultaneous EEG–fMRI data were acquired from 14 healthy, right-handed adult subjects (eight females, aged 26 ± 4 years).
source: Simultaneous EEG–fMRI data were acquired from 14 healthy, right-handed adult subjects (eight females, aged 26 ± 4 years).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the study participants.

claim: All subjects provided written informed consent.
source: All subjects provided written informed consent, and human subjects protocols were approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the National Institutes of Health and Vanderbilt University.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: Human subjects protocols were approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the National Institutes of Health and Vanderbilt University.
source: All subjects provided written informed consent, and human subjects protocols were approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the National Institutes of Health and Vanderbilt University.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: One scan was excluded due to a buffer overflow error in the EEG data acquisition.
source: One scan was excluded due to a buffer overflow error in the EEG data acquisition.
evidence: This is a factual statement about data exclusion.

claim: The analysis yielded a total of 23 scans (11 resting-state scans and 12 auditory task scans), each lasting 24.5 min.
source: This yielded a total of 23 scans (11 resting-state scans and 12 auditory task scans), each lasting 24.5 min.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the dataset.

claim: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Prisma scanner with a Siemens 64-channel head/neck coil.
source: MRI data were acquired on a 3T Siemens Prisma scanner (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) with a Siemens 64-channel head/neck coil.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: BOLD fMRI data were acquired with a multi-echo, gradient-echo EPI sequence.
source: BOLD fMRI data were acquired with a multi-echo, gradient-echo EPI sequence, with the following parameters: flip angle = 75 deg, TR = 2100 ms, echo times = 13.0, 29.4, and 45.7 ms, voxel size = 3 × 3 × 3 mm3, slice gap = 1 mm, matrix size = 82×50, 30 axial slices, acceleration factor = 2.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Scalp EEG was acquired simultaneously with fMRI using a 32-channel MR-compatible system at a sampling rate of 5 kHz.
source: Scalp EEG was acquired simultaneously with fMRI using a 32-channel MR-compatible system (BrainAmps MR, Brain Products GmbH) at a sampling rate of 5 kHz and was synchronized to the scanner's 10 MHz clock to facilitate reduction of MR gradient artifacts.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the EEG acquisition parameters.

claim: For the resting-state scans, subjects were instructed to keep their eyes closed and to stay awake as best as possible.
source: For the resting-state scans, subjects were instructed to keep their eyes closed and to stay awake as best as possible.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: For the auditory task, binaural tones were delivered with randomized inter-stimulus intervals.
source: For the auditory task, binaural tones were delivered (VisuaStim Digital; Resonance Technology, Northridge, CA) with randomized inter-stimulus intervals.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: Subjects were asked to make a right-handed button press as soon as possible upon hearing a tone.
source: Subjects were asked to make a right-handed button press as soon as possible upon hearing a tone (Lim and Dinges, 2008).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: Across all scans combined, 85.6% of epochs were rated as 'wake' by certified technologists using standard AASM criteria.
source: These ratings indicated that, across all scans combined, 85.6% of epochs were rated as 'wake', suggesting that subjects were mostly alert.
evidence: This is a factual statement from sleep staging analysis.

claim: It is likely that sleep was not a major factor in the experiments.
source: It is therefore likely state sleep was not a major factor in our experiments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sleep staging results.

claim: Multi-echo ICA denoising was carried out using tedana 0.0.9a.
source: Following this initial processing, multi-echo ICA denoising was carried out using tedana 0.0.9a (Elizabeth and Salo, 2020; Kundu et al., 2012; Kundu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the preprocessing method.

claim: Multi-echo ICA has proven effective in reducing head-motion effects.
source: While multi-echo independent component analysis (ICA) has proven effective in reducing head-motion effects (Kundu et al., 2013), we also ensured that scans with frame-to-frame head motion exceeding our voxel size (3 mm; corresponding to one resting-state and one task scan; Supplementary file 3) did not impact the major findings of this study.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kundu et al., 2013.

claim: Removing high-motion scans from the analysis had minimal impact on the correspondence between the fMRI alertness index with EEG and behavior.
source: Removing these high-motion scans from the analysis had minimal impact on the correspondence between the fMRI alertness index with EEG and behavior (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: A measure of alertness was computed from the EEG signal by taking the ratio of the root mean square (rms) amplitude in the 8–12 Hz range over the rms amplitude in the 3–7 Hz range (alpha/theta ratio).
source: A measure of alertness was computed from the EEG signal (averaged over channels P3, P4, Pz, O1, O2, Oz) within the 2.1 s interval of each fMRI time point (TR) by taking the ratio of the root mean square (rms) amplitude in the 8–12 Hz range over the rms amplitude in the 3–7 Hz range (alpha/theta ratio).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the EEG processing method.

claim: The alpha/theta ratio has previously been used in several human EEG–fMRI studies.
source: The alpha/theta ratio has previously been used in several human EEG–fMRI studies (Horovitz et al., 2008; Laufs et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Horovitz et al., 2008 and Laufs et al., 2006.

claim: The template map was constructed using the set of resting-state scans, and its performance was analyzed in the set of auditory task scans.
source: To allow for unbiased estimates of performance, the template map was constructed using the set of resting-state scans, and its performance was analyzed in the set of auditory task scans.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the cross-validation approach.

claim: Hits were further binned into an equal number of 'slow' and 'fast' trials, using a reaction-time threshold of 565 ms (median of responses pooled across all subjects).
source: Here, hits were further binned into an equal number of 'slow' and 'fast' trials, using a reaction-time threshold of 565 ms (median of responses pooled across all subjects).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the data analysis method.
